En un mundo donde la tecnología avanza a pasos agigantados, observamos cómo los robots comienzan a asumir tareas que antes parecían imposibles. En este video, un robot masilla las juntas de los paneles de yeso, demostrando precisión y eficiencia en cada movimiento, sea real o animado, nos invita a reflexionar:  En el futuro, los robots realizarán muchos de los trabajos difíciles, repetitivos y peligrosos que hoy enfrentamos. Pero hay algo que las máquinas no pueden replicar: nuestra creatividad, nuestra ética y nuestra capacidad de soñar.Los robots serán nuestros aliados, facilitando nuestras labores y permitiéndonos enfocarnos en lo que realmente importa. Seremos nosotros quienes diseñemos, innovemos y tomemos decisiones basadas en valores humanos.Mientras los robots se encargan del trabajo arduo, nosotros, los humanos, seguiremos liderando con imaginación y corazón. Porque aunque la tecnología avance, la chispa de la humanidad nunca será reemplazada.  ¿Qué opinas sobre el futuro de la tecnología en la construcción? artist and automata maker Amedeo Capelli, known as Stoccafisso Design, creates playful mechanical sculptures from wood, wire and simple mechanisms. In his recent shrimp automata, a handmade crustacean comes to life through a system of wooden gears, cams, rods and rotating parts hidden beneath the stage. Turning the crank transfers motion through the mechanism, making the shrimp’s body and limbs move in an exaggerated, almost theatrical way. Capelli’s work combines traditional automata-making, kinetic sculpture and humor. Instead of hiding the mechanics, he often leaves them visible, allowing us to understand how a simple rotation can be transformed into surprisingly complex movement. #shrimp #art #artist #niche #weird

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

In 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen rolled a cabinet into the court of Empress Maria Theresa in Vienna. On top sat a life-size wooden figure in a turban and robe. People called it "the Turk." Kempelen opened the doors one at a time to show the gears, then the Turk played chess and beat almost everyone. It toured Europe for decades. Benjamin Franklin played it in Paris and lost. In 1809 Napoleon played it at Schönbrunn. He made illegal moves. The Turk put the piece back each time, and on the third cheat it swept every piece off the board. The secret was a human chess master hidden inside. He slid on a seat from one side to the other as each door was opened. A candle lit his little board, and its smoke escaped through the Turk's turban. #history #weirdhistory #chess #napoleon #benjaminfranklin #robot #automation #animation #funnyhistory
